paper_title: Ropedia W0: Scaling Loco-Manipulation World Models across Embodiments with Human Experience

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: World models enable embodied agents to anticipate action consequences, yet jointly modeling locomotion and manipulation across diverse embodiments remains challenging due to heterogeneous action spaces and limited multimodal supervision. We present Ropedia W0, the first egocentric loco-manipulation world foundation model spanning humans and robots with diverse embodiments. We curate Xp-Data, comprising 10k hours of egocentric human data and 3k hours of robot data with unified multimodal annotations and systematic quality control. A unified kinematic representation encodes locomotion through camera poses and manipulation through projected skeletons, with robot skeletons combining embodiment-specific forward kinematics with extensive manual keypoint annotation and correction. We also introduce Xp-Teleop, a long-horizon loco-manipulation benchmark based on high-quality dexterous humanoid teleoperation data. Evaluations demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across five cross-embodiment benchmarks (DreamDojo, $Ψ_0$, $ω$-HOME, Xp-Teleop, and AgiBot) and on held-out human egocentric video, from zero-shot inference to few-shot and full-data post-training. Scaling human pre-training data improves performance on both human and robot evaluations. After distillation, our model supports real-time, minute-long rollouts, enabling live VR interaction. Applications in policy evaluation, model-based planning, and world-action modeling further demonstrate the model's utility for embodied decision-making.

Introduction World models predict how environments evolve in response to actions [42, 14] and support decision-making by imagining future outcomes [43], giving them considerable potential in embodied intelligence. However, most existing models [119, 122, 4] focus on fixed-base, gripperbased manipulation, leaving locomotion-induced viewpoint changes and dexterous handobject interactions largely underexplored. Moreover, generalizing across embodiments poses further challenge. DreamDojo [34] replaces latent-action conditioning with robot-specific actions during post-training, and Cosmos3 [1] relies on domain-specific action projections despite shared backbone; both therefore require dedicated control interface or additional adaptation for each new embodiment. Therefore, jointly modeling locomotion and manipulation while seamlessly generalizing across diverse embodiments remains an open problem. Learning generalizable world model hinges on large-scale, high-quality egocentric video paired with rich multimodal annotations, such as camera trajectories, hand motion, and task descriptions. While robot demonstrations across diverse tasks and embodiments remain expensive to collect, egocentric human video offers an abundant and complementary source of experience on how humans navigate and interact with their surroundings. However, existing public egocentric datasets [39, 40, 46, 113, 27, 2, 78] frequently suffer from incomplete or unreliable annotations. Specifically, many lack metric camera trajectories, provide noisy or missing hand poses, and adopt heterogeneous formats that hinder joint training. Furthermore, the scale of these datasets remains limited, falling short of the data required to train generalizable world model. To address these challenges, we present Ropedia W0, unified egocentric world model that scales learning from human and robot videos for cross-embodiment loco-manipulation. We curate Xp-Data, comprising 10k hours of egocentric human data and 3k hours of robot data, with unified geometric, kinematic, and semantic annotations produced through automated processing, manual robot-keypoint annotation, and quality checks. To connect human motion and robot actions, we introduce shared explicit kinematic representation that combines metric camera poses for locomotion-induced viewpoint changes with projected skeletons for manipulation. The skeletons combine human pose annotations with robot forward kinematics (FK) and manually annotated or corrected robot keypoints, preserving embodiment-specific structure in an image-aligned format. This conditioning interface remains consistent across human pre-training, humanrobot mid-training, and optional post-training. We further introduce Xp-Teleop, humanoid teleoperation benchmark for evaluating long-horizon prediction during locomotion and dexterous manipulation. We evaluate Ropedia W0 on five cross-embodiment benchmarks (DreamDojo, Ψ0, ω-HOME, Xp-Teleop, and AgiBot), alongside held-out human egocentric video. Results demonstrate strong predictive performance across embodiments and post-training budgets, including zero-shot transfer and data-efficient adaptation. Scaling analyses show that increasing the amount of human pre-training data improves both prediction on human videos and transfer to robots. Ablations establish the complementary roles of camera and skeleton conditioning, while distillation enables real-time, minute-long rollouts and live VR interaction across embodiments. Downstream experiments further demonstrate accurate policy ranking, improved trajectory planning, and more robust action learning in simulation and on real robots. Our contributions are threefold: We introduce Ropedia W0, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first unified egocentric world model for cross-embodiment loco-manipulation. shared explicit kinematic representation of camera poses and projected skeletons enables scalable learning from human and robot videos. We design human-in-the-loop pipeline that unifies collection, annotation, and quality checks, including extensive manual robot-keypoint annotation and correction of inaccurate FK projections. Consequently, we build Xp-Data, comprising over 10k hours of human data and 3k hours of robot data in shared schema. Extensive experiments show that Ropedia W0 achieves state-of-the-art cross-embodiment prediction, including on our long-horizon loco-manipulation Xp-Teleop benchmark. We further show that Ropedia W0s performance scales with human data and demonstrate applications in real-time interaction, policy evaluation, model-based planning, and world action modeling. 2. Related Work Robotic video world models. Early world models learned compact latent dynamics for control [42, 43]; large video generators yield interactive worlds [14, 88, 89, 75, 24, 74] and ego-motion-controlled driving simulators [47, 98, 35]. Distillation and self-rollout training convert video generators into causal few-step models [130, 50, 26, 72], augmented with longhorizon memory [45, 100]. Robotic world models learn video dynamics from robot trajectories [124, 142, 55, 67, 41, 139, 122, 44], often adapting video foundation model [3, 108]. Numerical action tokens require embodiment-specific encoding [111, 41]; latent actions inferred from video [14, 128, 36, 38, 34] make unlabeled footage usable, but may entangle actions with other visual changes [133]; spatially aligned renderings provide explicit geometric conditioning [55, 122, 126, 115, 119]. Cross-embodiment models use embodiment-specific action heads, 3 projections, or adaptation [111, 34, 1], single rendered interface [115, 119], or factorized humanto-robot recomposition [22]. The last, AnyWorld [22], recomposes human interactions into robot experiences but conditions on source human skeletons rather than target-robot kinematics and is evaluated mainly on manipulation, leaving sustained loco-manipulation untested. Ego-motion is also studied in navigation and driving [8, 47] and in egocentric predictors conditioned on or jointly modeling full-body pose [7, 87, 121]. Ropedia W0 uses an explicit kinematic interface to unify loco-manipulation across humans, gripper robots, and dexterous humanoids. Human and robot datasets. Large egocentric human collections cover daily and skilled activity [39, 27, 40]; pose-annotated collections add body or hand pose [82, 78, 46, 92], and portable rigs bring hand pose into everyday scenes [109, 76]. Aggregated and in-the-wild demonstrations [86, 58, 107, 30, 118] and large teleoperation sets [15] provide robot actions, calibrated views and task captions in varying combinations, with substantial coverage of tabletop arm and gripper manipulation; humanoid sets include locomotion or dexterous hands [138, 101, 94, 117, 65]. Evaluation data include held-out robot video clips [142, 34, 119], multimodal world-model benchmarks [1], and benchmarks measuring visual quality, physical consistency or embodied utility [132, 84]. Xp-Data unifies annotations for public human and robot data and self-collected egocentric video; Xp-Teleop benchmarks long-horizon dexterous humanoid loco-manipulation with robot-native kinematics. Policy evaluation, planning, and learning. Policy evaluation extends real-to-sim protocols [62] to video world models through recorded-action rollouts [142, 64, 119] or closed-loop policy interaction [95, 41, 103, 102]. For planning, world models score or refine action proposals using predicted outcomes [93, 28, 53, 34], in pixel or learned latent spaces [140, 5], and support reinforcement fine-tuning and synthetic data generation [143, 56, 61, 120, 54]. Vision-languageaction models map observations and language to actions using pretrained vision-language models [13, 59, 12, 52, 11], increasingly trained with human video [128, 16, 15, 123, 80, 57, 117], whereas worldaction models couple future video or latent-state prediction with action learning [21, 141, 48, 111, 67, 127, 1, 9, 81, 65, 112, 131]. Ropedia W0 supports these applications in Sec. 6; for worldaction modeling, we transfer its pretrained video backbone to initialize such model rather than adding dedicated action head. 3. Data Learning cross-embodiment loco-manipulation requires data that captures both viewpoint changes and manipulator motion under shared annotation scheme. However, existing datasets [39, 40, 46, 113, 27, 2, 78, 31, 29, 60, 77, 37, 92, 97, 15, 58, 30, 135, 101, 11, 33, 10, 63, 85, 49, 105, 138] fall short of this requirement: most lack essential geometric information such as camera poses, and their hand annotations are often noisy or inaccurate, making them insufficient for training general-purpose world model. To address this gap, our human-in-the-loop data pipeline unifies collection, multimodal annotation, and quality checks  (Fig. 2)  . We re-annotate public human and robot recordings, with substantial manual robot-keypoint annotation and correction, and collect over 6,000 hours of in-house multi-view video with four-fisheye-camera rig. This yields Xp-Data, over 10k human and 3k robot training hours with synchronized RGB, camera trajectories, manipulator skeletons, and captions; wrist poses and wide-FOV skeletons are included where available. Our Xp-Teleop benchmark provides about one held-out hour of long-horizon dexterous humanoid loco-manipulation, recorded in the same schema with an off-the-shelf rig [104] (Sec. A.2). Model Ropedia W0 combines unified kinematic control interface with video diffusion model for cross-embodiment egocentric loco-manipulation prediction  (Fig. 4)  . The interface jointly captures viewpoint changes and manipulation through camera poses and projected skeletons, allowing human and robot motion to share common visual format while preserving embodiment-specific geometry. We first formulate the prediction task and introduce shared representation of camera and manipulator motion (Sec. 4.1). We then describe the conditioning architecture (Sec. 4.2), training recipe (Sec. 4.3), and distillation (Sec. 4.4). 4.1. Training: From Human Experience to Cross-Embodiment We train Ropedia W0 in two stages: human pre-training and humanrobot mid-training. Both stages share the camera-and-skeleton conditioning interface, enabling the model to transfer motion-conditioned prediction learned from human videos to diverse robot embodiments. Human pre-training. We first train on large-scale egocentric human videos conditioned on text, camera trajectories, and projected hand skeletons. This stage learns the visual consequences of camera and manipulator motion across diverse environments and interactions, establishing foundation for cross-embodiment transfer. Humanrobot mid-training. We continue training on balanced mixture of human and robot data, sampling each with equal probability. Robot motion is expressed through the same conditioning interface using embodiment-native kinematics. This stage introduces robot-specific appearance, manipulator geometry, and interaction patterns while maintaining exposure to diverse human experience. We also incorporate wrist-pose and wide-FOV skeleton conditions during this stage, using availability gates to accommodate samples with different annotation coverage. 4.4. Xp-Teleop Xp-Teleop is humanoid teleoperation benchmark for evaluating long-horizon prediction during locomotion and dexterous manipulation. It comprises 27 long-horizon takes (about one hour of egocentric video at 30 fps) recorded on Unitree G1 humanoid with two six-DoF dexterous hands through whole-body teleoperation rig assembled from off-the-shelf hardware and Unitrees open-source framework [104]. Two operators drive locomotion and manipulation concurrently, so walking and dexterous interaction occur within the same take. Every take is recorded with synchronized RGB-D, camera poses, projected skeletons, robot states, language, tactile, and head-IMU signals in the same schema as Xp-Data, and is divided into 543 humanannotated atomic segments spanning 30 skill classes (median 18 segments per take). We keep failed grasps and recoveries so that the benchmark also probes whether world model can simulate off-nominal outcomes, not only successful executions. Fig. 5 overviews the activities, representative episodes, synchronized modalities, and action labels, and Table 1 compares Xp-Teleop with other humanoid teleoperation datasets in task coverage and available modalities. Each take is long-horizon episode that chains locomotion with manipulation, such as putting objects into box or folding jacket on the bed (b). Takes are recorded as single synchronized multimodal stream (egocentric RGB-D, 6-DoF camera pose, projected hand/robot skeletons and masks, 29-joint robot state, time-aligned language segments, per-hand tactile, and head IMU; c), and their 543 annotated segments are dominated by loco-manipulation verbs such as reach, walk, and grasp (d). 6. Experiments 6.1. Setup Benchmarks. We evaluate action-conditioned video prediction on five cross-embodiment benchmarks spanning distinct embodiments and data sources: (i) the DreamDojo benchmarks [34], three Fourier GR-1 robot evaluation sets from DreamDojo: In-lab (100 clips), EgoDex (65 clips), and DreamDojo-HV (68 clips); (ii) Ψ0 [117], 100 evaluation windows of dexterous humanoid manipulation recorded with the Ψ0 vision-language-action (VLA) system (50 seen-task, 50 unseen-task); (iii) ω-HOME [65], 100 evaluation windows of household loco-manipulation on Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous five-finger hands across 24 tasks (50 seen, 50 from five held-out tasks); (iv) Xp-Teleop (Sec. 5), 100 evaluation windows of long-horizon dexterous humanoid teleoperation, split by scene (50 windows from held-out takes of training scenes, 50 from unseen scenes); and (v) AgiBot [15], 50 held-out windows of gripper-based manipulation, where all compared models include AgiBot data in training. In addition, we report zero-shot prediction on 200 held-out human egocentric clips (EgoSuite and OpenAoE; Sec. 6.2). Metrics. We report visual quality with PSNR, SSIM [116], and LPIPS [134]. For benchmarks with camera motion we additionally evaluate camera-trajectory accuracy on poses recovered from the generated video, namely absolute trajectory error (ATE), relative pose error (RPE), and relative rotation error (RRE), as well as hand-following accuracy via keypoint PCK@0.1 (PCKm on matched hands, with detection rate Det). Where noted, we also report video-quality metrics (VBench [51] subject/background consistency, dynamic degree, and aesthetic quality) and FVD [106]. Full metric definitions and the per-benchmark evaluation protocol are given in Sec. C.1. 11 Post-training protocol. For each benchmark, we evaluate three adaptation settings: no posttraining (direct transfer), few-shot post-training using small number of episodes per training task, and full-data post-training using the entire training split. Throughout, zero-shot (equivalently no post-training / direct transfer) means the model is evaluated on target dataset it was never trained on. The target embodiment may still appear in the multi-embodiment mid-training mixture through other datasets, but the target evaluation dataset itself is never used for training. Seen vs. unseen splits within benchmark refer to seen vs. held-out tasks/scenes of that benchmark, not to the embodiment. We evaluate both training stages of Ropedia W0: pretrain rows are initialized from the human-only pre-training stage, and midtrain rows from the subsequent mid-training stage that mixes human and multi-embodiment robot data. Checkpoints are always selected on held-out validation split, never on the benchmark itself. Baselines. We compare against generalist robot world models with different action interfaces: DreamDojo (2B and 14B), which conditions on continuous latent actions pretrained from largescale human video, and Cosmos3 (Nano, 16B; Super, 64B), which treats action as first-class modality with per-domain action encoders. On the egocentric human-video and AgiBot benchmarks we additionally report two recent action-conditioned world models where available, OSCAR [119] and RynnWorld-Teleop [136]. For data-efficiency comparisons, we additionally post-train the same architecture as ours initialized from the public video-generation weights (official base), isolating the contribution of our pre-training. All baselines are post-trained with their official recipes. 6.2. Benchmark Results Human egocentric video. We evaluate on 200 clips from EgoSuite [68] and OpenAoE [66], two datasets unseen during training by both Ropedia W0 and all compared methods. Ropedia W0 achieves the lowest camera-trajectory errors, the highest hand-following accuracy, and the best visual quality (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS)  (Table 2)  . Conclusion We presented Ropedia W0, unified egocentric world model for loco-manipulation across humans and robots with grippers or dexterous hands. Its explicit kinematic representation combines camera poses for viewpoint motion with projected skeletons for manipulation, preserving embodiment-native geometry within shared visual format. This interface enables learning from human and robot data and remains consistent from pre-training to post-training. Trained on Xp-Data with 10k hours of human video and 3k hours of robot data, Ropedia W0 demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization, data-efficient adaptation, and competitive prediction across diverse benchmarks, including our new Xp-Teleop. Our scaling analysis further shows that increasing human-video pre-training improves prediction on held-out human video and transfer to robot benchmarks, highlighting human experience as scalable source of supervision for cross-embodiment world modeling. Beyond video prediction, the model supports policy evaluation, model-based planning, and worldaction modeling, while distillation enables real-time interactive simulation.

Data and Benchmark Details We first document the curated training corpus and its unified annotations, then describe the held-out Xp-Teleop benchmark, including its collection setup and dataset-comparison criteria. A.1. Data Curation and Annotation Examples Figure S1 summarizes the curation pipeline. The examples below illustrate the resulting scene coverage and unified motion annotations. Figure S1 Data curation funnel for Xp-Data. Robot and human egocentric recordings pass through source screening, motion annotation, and quality control; gray bands mark data removed at each step, and the surviving streams form the unified corpus of 3,000 robot hours and 10,000 human hours. Figures S2S4 visualize the corpus across human and robot recordings. Figure S3 shows example robot frames spanning different environments, tasks, objects, and embodiments. Figures S2 and S4 overlay the unified motion annotations on the same kinds of frames: projected hand or manipulator skeletons in the image, with the per-window camera trajectory shown in the inset. 28 Figure S2 Motion annotations on the egocentric human data. Projected 21-point hand skeletons are overlaid on each frame, with the two hands drawn in different colors; the inset shows the camera trajectory of the surrounding window. 29 Figure S3 Example frames from the robot data in Xp-Data. The grid spans dexterous five-finger hands, three-finger hands, and parallel grippers on single-arm, dual-arm, and humanoid platforms, across household, retail, industrial, and tabletop scenes. 30 Figure S4 Motion annotations on the robot data. Image-aligned skeletons combine embodiment-native FK projections with manual keypoint annotation and correction (Sec. 3), covering dexterous hands and grippers; the inset shows the camera trajectory of the surrounding window. 31 A.2. Xp-Teleop Collection and Benchmark Details The benchmark overview  (Fig. 5)  and the dataset comparison  (Table 1)  appear in the main text (Sec. 5); here we provide the full rig, control, recording, and comparison details. Rig. Unitree G1 humanoid with 29 actuated degrees of freedom is equipped with two Inspire RH56DFX dexterous hands, each with six actuated degrees of freedom. An Azure Kinect DK mounted on custom 3D-printed helmet rigidly attached to the robots head records the egocentric RGB-D view. Because the G1 has no actuated neck joints, the camera moves only with the waist and mobile base, matching the motion represented by our camera-pose control channel (Sec. 4). Control. Two operators control the robot concurrently, allowing locomotion and manipulation to occur within the same take. The manipulation operator wears Meta Quest 3, whose controller-free hand tracking provides targets to Pinocchio-based inverse-kinematics solver for the two 7-DoF arms and to dexterous-hand retargeting module. The locomotion operator independently commands the robots base velocity using Unitrees R3 remote. Recording. Each take records the robot and hand joint states, commanded targets, R3 commands, headset tracking, and Kinect stream on common clock. From these signals, we derive the two action channels described in Sec. 4: camera poses and hand skeletons. The hand skeletons are computed through forward kinematics and projected into the image using the calibrated helmet-to-camera extrinsics. We retain every take initiated by the operators, including failed grasps and subsequent recoveries, because Xp-Teleop is intended to evaluate whether world model can simulate off-nominal outcomes as well as successful executions. Dataset composition and annotation granularity. Xp-Teleop contains 27 long-horizon teleoperation takes, totaling approximately one hour of egocentric video recorded at 30 fps. The takes are divided into 543 human-annotated atomic segments, with each take containing between 8 and 42 segments (median 18). This annotation is substantially finer-grained than the common convention of assigning single instruction to an entire episode. The resulting segments cover 30 skill classes. The segment captions also identify the manipulated objects and describe the temporal progression of each task, providing language supervision aligned with the recorded observations and actions. Scope of the dataset comparison. Table 1 compares publicly described dexterous-humanoid teleoperation datasets in terms of robot capabilities, task horizon, and available recording modalities. We divide the datasets into two groups according to how the lower body is used during data collection. In the tabletop-teleoperation group, the robots legs remain locked even if the release provides base commands or whole-body state. In the loco-manipulation group, locomotion is actively commanded and can occur within the same episode as manipulation. Task-horizon metrics. The three task-horizon columns report episode-level means over the analyzed portion of each dataset. Duration is the wall-clock length of one episode, computed as the number of recorded frames divided by the datasets frame rate (30 Hz for all datasets except GR00T-Teleop, 20 Hz). Frame counts are taken from each datasets own metadata. For our dataset we report the released task windows, not the raw recordings. RoboMIND does not document its frame rate; we assume 30 Hz. Loco. Range measures how much space an episode covers. For each episode we take the 3-D position trajectory of the robot base (or, when only camera trajectory is available, the head camera), compute its axis-aligned bounding box, and report the box diagonal in metres. We use the bounding-box diagonal rather than integrated path length, because path length at 30 Hz is dominated by body sway and pose-estimation jitter (on our data it inflates the value by roughly 7). Pose sources. Ours: visual-inertial SLAM (metric). Humanoid-Everyday: on-board odometry. UnifoLM-WBT (new schema): the robot state estimators base pose. All other datasets provide no metric base pose; we run DA3-Streaming with its metric configuration on the egocentric video (10 fps, 504 px input) to obtain camera poses. Because monocular metric SLAM has systematic scale error, we calibrate it once against ground truth: on the 879 Humanoid-Everyday locomotion episodes the DA3 box diagonal exceeds the odometry value by median factor of 1.39 (IQR 1.281.55), and on our 27 episodes the median factor against SLAM is 1.03; we divide all DA3-derived values by the pooled median 1.39. After calibration the estimator reproduces ground truth within 10% on both datasets (ours 1.48 vs 1.61 m; Humanoid-Everyday 0.84 vs 0.82 m). For AgiBot-Beta we estimate on length-stratified sample of 30 episodes. Unitree G1 Dex1/Dex3, PH2D, and RoboMIND Tien Kung are reported as 0. Subtasks counts how many sequential sub-goals an episodes task instruction specifies. We apply one rule to every dataset: the instruction is lower-cased and split into clauses at commas, semicolons, periods and the connectives "and", "then", "until", "upon", "after"; clause counts as one subtask if its first or second content word is an action verb from fixed list (pick, place, put, take, grasp, carry, walk, go, enter, turn, open, close, push, pull, pour, wipe, fold, locate, find, hang, press, insert, . . . ). Locomotion clauses count the same as manipulation clauses. Every instruction counts at least 1. Instruction sources: the per-episode task string for LeRobot datasets, the HDF5 description attribute for PH2D and RoboMIND, the task name for ω-HOME, and the human-written task instruction of each take for our dataset (one 19-step instruction excluded as an outlier). AgiBot-Beta ships no instruction text. Because subtask boundaries follow the wording and granularity of each releases instructions, this count is an annotation-level measure of task horizon rather than platform-independent action count. Modality criteria. The modality columns describe information available in the analyzed dataset release. For Kpts., we also count image-space keypoints that can be reconstructed from released joint states and camera calibration using publicly available URDF. RGB@fps reports the resolution and frame rate of the principal egocentric RGB stream. Dpt. requires usable released depth stream; placeholder or zero-filled channels do not qualify. IMU requires explicit inertial-sensor measurements. Estimated root poses, torso poses, or camera trajectories alone are not counted as IMU data. Tac. denotes released tactile measurements. WB joints requires recorded joint states covering both the upper and lower body, including the legs. Arm-only or hand-only states, estimated root or torso poses, and commanded base velocities do not satisfy this criterion. This column describes the coverage of the recorded state and does not require the leg joints to exhibit substantial motion during the released episodes. Consequently, dataset may provide whole-body joint states while still belonging to the tabletop group. Cal. requires sufficient camera calibration to relate robot kinematics to the image observations, including both camera intrinsics and the relevant extrinsics. Camera trajectories or extrinsics provided without intrinsics do not satisfy this criterion. Kpts. denotes temporally aligned image-space keypoints, either provided directly or obtainable by projecting the relevant robot kinematics using released joint states, sufficient camera 33 calibration, and publicly available URDF. Dataset-specific qualifications. For Unitree Dex1, whole-body joint states are available only in the v3 release; v2 provides arm and gripper states but not the corresponding lower-body joint states. Although v3 supports base commands, the observed variation of its leg joints is below 0.03 rad in the analyzed recordings. We therefore treat its measured locomotion range as zero and place it in the tabletop group. Ψ0 supports locomotion, but the analyzed release does not provide leg-joint states. Its released depth channel is zero-filled and is therefore not counted as usable depth. RoboMIND entries refer specifically to its Xsens dexterous-hand subset. This subset includes depth observations but does not provide hand-joint states. Humanoid Everyday task-horizon statistics are computed from its loco-manipulation subset, and its tactile measurements are available only for the G1/Dex3 embodiment. The analyzed ω-HOME files do not contain depth stream. B. Model and Implementation Details This section describes the video backbones, distillation and interactive inference, and the optional wide-FOV skeleton-conditioning branch. Figures and measurements are grouped with the component they illustrate. B.1. Backbone and Conditioning Ropedia W0 predicts future egocentric video from an initial visual observation and factorized camera and manipulator controls (Sec. 4.1). The following details describe the pretrained backbones used by this shared conditioning interface. Latent video diffusion backbones. We instantiate Ropedia W0 at two scales using the Wan2.2 family of pretrained video diffusion models [108]. Wan2.2-TI2V-5B uses dense diffusion transformer with approximately 5B parameters. Wan2.2-I2V-A14B uses two experts specialized for different noise regimes: high-noise expert and low-noise expert. Only one expert is active at each denoising step, yielding approximately 14B active parameters. In our experiments, the two experts are adapted separately and used in their respective noise regimes during inference. Both backbones operate on spatiotemporal latents produced by video VAE and follow the diffusion transformer architecture [90]. Text embeddings are incorporated through crossattention, while sinusoidal timestep embeddings provide adaptive normalization and residual modulation within each transformer block. We train them with the latent flow-matching objective [70]: the video VAE encodes each clip into latents, the first temporal latent is retained as clean visual context, and noise and the loss are applied only to future latents. The camera-ray and skeleton conditioning branches introduced in Sec. 4.2 augment these backbones through zero-initialized projections, preserving the pretrained models behavior at initialization. B.2. Distillation and Interactive Simulation Distillation recipe. We first obtain 4-step autoregressive generator using Causal Forcing [144, 137], then extend it to long-video streaming using LongLive [125], retaining cameraskeleton conditioning. Few-step distillation. An autoregressive diffusion model provides causal initialization. Asymmetric DMD then trains the causal generator using frozen bidirectional real-score teacher (with classifier-free guidance) and an online bidirectional fake-score model. The generator starts from the causal initialization, while both score networks initialize from the bidirectional camera skeleton model. The fake-score model learns denoising objective on generated samples. Long-video extension. LongLive adapts the few-step generator for streaming with within-block bidirectional and cross-block causal attention. bounded KV cache retains local window and an attention sink. Figure S5 illustrates distillation; Fig. S6 shows subsequent long-video streaming. Figure S5 Distillation of Ropedia W0 into few-step causal student. Top: causal distillation initializes the few-step autoregressive generator. Bottom: asymmetric DMD updates the causal generator Gθ using frozen bidirectional real-score teacher and an online-trained bidirectional fake-score model. The diagram illustrates the A14B MoE backbone; the 5B model follows an analogous procedure with dense backbone. LongLive subsequently extends the few-step model for long-video streaming (Fig. S6). 35 Interactive inference and throughput. On single GPU at 640 480, the 4-step student generates 125-frame clip in about 2 of autoregressive generation and about 6 including VAE decoding (21 fps), compared with about 41 for the 50-step teacher (a 7 end-to-end speed-up), and streams its first block within roughly 1.4 s. Figure S6 illustrates the streaming rollout mechanism; Table S1 reports quality and throughput across rollout lengths. Figure S6 LongLive-based streaming with the distilled student. Successive segments reuse the previously generated visual context while accepting updated controls (skeleton, camera trajectory, and text). Each block is produced by the few-step causal student, so the per-segment cost is bounded while retained context carries information across segments, enabling real-time long-horizon rollout. On the WorldArena [99] (RoboTwin 2.0) test set, the narrow skeleton touches the image border in 99.4% of frames; 1.5 field-of-view render raises in-frame manipulator coverage from 0.37 to 0.56. The optional wide-FOV branch (Sec. 4.2) feeds this render through per-block cross-attention, providing arm configuration that is absent from the narrow view. Evaluation Protocols We specify the human-video evaluation procedure and the protocol used for the scaling curves. Supplementary benchmark results are collected in Sec. D. C.1. Human Egocentric Video Evaluation The pooled 200-clip results (100 per dataset from EgoSuite [68] and OpenAoE [66]) are reported in the main text  (Table 2)  . Here we specify the evaluation-set composition, protocol, and metric definitions; the per-dataset breakdown is reported in Sec. D.1. Evaluation set. We evaluate on 100 clips per dataset (200 total), sampled across high, medium, and low camera-motion strata. Evaluation protocol. Clips contain 81 frames at 640 480 and 16 fps. Methods receive the same initial frame and, when supported, the same caption, with seed 0. Camera and hand conditions derive from the same camera annotations and projected hand keypoints, converted to each methods native interface. Each baseline is run under its native conditioning interface: DreamDojo with latent actions, Cosmos3 with joint camera-and-hand conditioning. Metrics. ATE is absolute trajectory error after rigid SE(3) alignment without scale fitting; RPE measures stepwise translation error, and RRE measures rotation error relative to the first frame. Camera poses are estimated from generated videos with DA3 [69]. Hand metrics use MediaPipe [79] detections at confidence 0.3, matched to projected annotations. PCK@.1 uses threshold of 10% of the image diagonal and penalizes missed detections; PCKm@.1 evaluates matched hands only, and Det is the detection rate. Cons., Dyn, and Aes denote VBench subject consistency, dynamic degree, and aesthetic quality. FVD16 uses non-overlapping 16-frame windows, while FVDfull uses the full sequences. FVD is recomputed for each evaluation set rather than averaged across datasets. In the human evaluation tables, ATE and RPE are reported in centimeters, RRE in degrees, HandL2 in pixels, and PSNR in dB. PCK, PCKm, Det, Cons., Dyn, and Aes are reported as percentages; SSIM, LPIPS, and FVD have no physical units. C.2. Scaling Protocol The scaling figures appear in the main text: held-out human video at hand-detection confidence 0.3  (Fig. 6)  , human-to-robot transfer to Ψ0/Xp-Teleop/ω-HOME  (Fig. 7)  , and the DreamDojo cross-evaluation sets  (Fig. 8)  . We detail the shared protocol here. Each point is checkpoint taken at the indicated amount of human-video pre-training data (hours of video processed), with the data mixture held fixed. Because training stays within single epoch, the hours processed at each point equal the amount of unique human data seen, so these curves measure data scaling rather than repeated exposure. For held-out human video the checkpoint is evaluated zero-shot, whereas for the DreamDojo and transfer benchmarks it is post-trained on the target with the same recipe before evaluation. For transfer scaling, post-training uses one clip for 50 steps on Ψ0 and 144 clips for five epochs on Xp-Teleop. 39 D. E. Qualitative Comparisons We group qualitative comparisons by evaluation setting. Compared methods receive the same initial frame and conditioning through their native interfaces. Ground-truth and predicted frames are aligned in time; figures from the project-page videos use the same displayed frame indices across methods. E.1. Cross-Embodiment Robot Prediction Figures S10S12 compare predictions on held-out clips from Fourier, AgiBot, Baihu, Dexora, RH20T, and DROID. These examples cover different manipulators, objects, and interaction types; the captions specify the adaptation setting. Figure S10 Robot-dataset comparisons (1/3). (a) Fourier: putting tape in bag; (b) AgiBot: grasping desk fan. These are held-out clips: Ropedia W0 uses mid-training and Cosmos3 uses fine-tuning on the robot mixture. Colored skeletons are supplied input conditions overlaid on the generated frames. 45 Figure S11 Robot-dataset comparisons (2/3). (a) Baihu: placing hot dog in bowl; (b) Dexora: arranging fruit. Columns compare the ground truth, Ropedia W0, Cosmos3-Nano, and Cosmos3-Super at aligned frames. The held-out-clip setting and input skeleton overlays follow Fig. S10. 46 Figure S12 Robot-dataset comparisons (3/3). (a) RH20T: turning steering wheel; (b) DROID: closing door. These examples extend the comparison to gripper motion and interactions with articulated objects. The held-out-clip setting and input skeleton overlays follow Fig. S10. E.2. Zero-Shot Loco-Manipulation Figures S13 and S14 compare zero-shot predictions on household tasks from ω-HOME [65], held-out loco-manipulation dataset not used in training by the compared models. The examples show generated hand motion, object interactions, and scene appearance against time-aligned ground-truth frames. Figure S13 Zero-shot comparisons on ω-HOME (1/2). (a) Reaching into the upper fridge; (b) pushing chair. The compared models have not been trained on ω-HOME. Rows show aligned frames from the same clip; colored skeletons are input conditions overlaid on each generated video. 48 Figure S14 Zero-shot comparisons on ω-HOME (2/2). (a) Putting an apple in fruit basket; (b) sorting fruit from office supplies. Ground-truth frames provide reference for the generated hand and object configurations. The setting and input skeleton overlays follow Fig. S13. E.3. Post-Training and Data Efficiency Adaptation on ω-HOME. Figure S15 compares zero-shot and post-trained predictions against the baselines on manipulation task. Figure S15 ω-HOME [65] manipulation task (fruit-bucket arrangement). Left: zero-shot; right: after post-training. Ropedia W0 follows the commanded hands and matches the ground truth in both settings, whereas the baselines lose the arm or drift. Pretrained initialization under limited data. We probe data efficiency by post-training on only 1% of the GR-1 data from two initializations: our pretrained base versus public video-generation weights (Wan2.2-I2V-A14B). Across both the In-lab (Fig. S16) and EgoDex (Fig. S17) settings, initializing from our pretrained base yields markedly sharper predictions and preserves object and hand detail that the public base loses. 50 Figure S16 Few-shot data efficiency on GR-1 (In-lab). Both models are post-trained on 1% of the data; Ropedia W0 initializes from our pretrained base and Wan2.2-I2V-A14B [108] from public video-generation weights. Our base yields markedly sharper, more faithful predictions. Figure S17 Few-shot data efficiency on GR-1 (EgoDex [46]). Same 1% budget; initializing from our pretrained base preserves object and hand detail that the public base loses. 51 Post-training data budgets. Colored skeletons are overlaid input conditions. Each row uses the same frame index across settings. 52 E.4. Additional Long-Horizon Rollouts Figure S19 shows two additional 32-second generated sequences with their supplied camera and hand conditions. These examples visualize rollout continuity; the quantitative long-horizon comparisons are reported in Sec. D.3. Figure S19 Additional 32-second generated rollouts. (a) Collecting fruit from closet; (b) picking up bok choy. Each sequence starts with the input image at 0 s, followed by generated frames sampled every 6.4 s, read left to right and then top to bottom. The camera and hand-pose insets display supplied conditions. 53 F. Limitations and Future Work 1. The distilled student supports real-time, minute-long rollouts (Sec. B.2); stronger memory mechanisms or periodic re-grounding are promising directions for extending stable interactive simulation to longer horizons. 2. We study up to 14B-active model and scale the amount of human-video pre-training data while holding the data mixture fixed; prediction quality improves monotonically with the amount of data (Sec. C.2), suggesting that scaling data and model size further, and broadening embodiment and task coverage, are promising directions toward more capable and reliable embodied world models. 3. Our kinematic interface captures camera and manipulator motion but not physical contact or object dynamics; coupling the world model with simulation-ready, physically grounded 3D assets and scenes [1820] is promising direction toward modeling the underlying dynamics rather than only their visual consequences.
